The project can be checked for validity to identify potential problems that would prevent the workflows from being executed: does every reference resolve, are no required fields missing, are there any duplicated id. `validateProject()` does this and prints a readable report. This guide shows how to run it, read the report, act on a problem, and gate a script on the result.

It assumes you know what a Project is and how to create one (see `vignette("how-to-set-up-a-project")` and `vignette("how-to-design-scenarios")`).

Run it right after you finish editing and before running. `runScenarios()`, `buildSimulations()`, `createDataCombined()`, `createPlots()` and `runPI()` each check the parts of the project they use before any simulation starts, and stop with a list of every critical error they find there. They do not show warnings, and they do not look at the other parts of the project. An explicit `validateProject()` gives you the whole picture: every section, warnings included. `vignette("about-the-project-model")` covers why validation is split up this way and why it reports two levels of finding.

Throughout, work on a writable copy of the bundled example:

```{r}
project_dir <- withr::local_tempdir()
initProject(destination = project_dir, type = "example", createExcel = FALSE)
project <- loadProject(file.path(project_dir, "Project.json"))
```

## Read a report

A report separates two kinds of finding, and which one you got decides whether you have to act:

- A **critical error** blocks. A duplicate id, a required field left empty, or a reference to something that does not exist. `isAnyCriticalErrors()` returns `TRUE`, and the operations that use that part of the project will not run until you fix it.
- A **warning** does not block. It is surfaced so you see it, and a section with warnings and no critical errors is still valid.

The quickest single question, "is anything blocking?", is `isAnyCriticalErrors()`.

Passing `validate = FALSE` to `runScenarios()` or `createPlots()` skips their check and lets a scenario build on whatever the model file already carries. Reach for it only when you know the gap is deliberate.

## Validate a clean project

The bundled example is well formed, so its report is short. `validateProject()` runs every section validator plus a cross-reference pass and returns a structured object that prints a summary:

```{r}
results <- validateProject(project)
results
```

`isAnyCriticalErrors()` agrees:

```{r}
isAnyCriticalErrors(results)
```

## Diagnose a dangling reference

The most common slip is a dangling reference: a definition pointing at an id that does not exist, usually a small misspelling. Note that a *loaded* project can hold one even though `addScenario()` would have refused it, because reading a project reports gaps rather than rejecting them (`vignette("about-the-project-model")` explains why).

To see what the report looks like, suppose one scenario file in our copy mistypes the individual id `adult_male` as `adlt_male`. Reloading the project catches the dangling reference at load time, and `validateProject()` then reports it in full:

```{r, echo = FALSE}
scenario_file <- file.path(
  project_dir,
  "definitions",
  "scenarios",
  "aciclovir_iv.json"
)
text <- readLines(scenario_file)
text <- gsub('"adult_male"', '"adlt_male"', text, fixed = TRUE)
writeLines(text, scenario_file)

broken <- suppressWarnings(loadProject(file.path(project_dir, "Project.json")))
```

The report is grouped by definition type, and the references from one definition to another that do not resolve are listed together under `crossReferences`. A cross (`✖`) marks each critical error, an exclamation mark (`!`) marks each warning, and the sections with nothing to report collapse into a single tail line.

```{r}
broken_results <- validateProject(broken)
broken_results
```

Notice the message does not just say the reference is missing; it offers a **"did you mean"** suggestion built from the ids that actually exist (`did you mean 'adult_male'?`), the validator catching the most common mistake, a small misspelling of an existing id.

## Read the result in code

The printed report is for you; the object `validateProject()` returns is for your code. It is a named list with one entry per definition type, plus `crossReferences`, which holds every reference from one definition to another that does not resolve. Each entry holds the critical errors and warnings for that part of the project, so a script can read them without parsing any text. The misspelled individual id is reported under `crossReferences`, not under `scenarios`:

```{r}
names(broken_results)
broken_results$crossReferences$critical_errors[[1]]$message
```

`validationSummary()` rolls the per-section results into aggregate counts and the names of the sections that produced errors or warnings, which is handy for a one-line status in a report or a log:

```{r}
validationSummary(broken_results)
```

## Resolve and re-validate

Fixing the problem uses the same functions you already know. Here the scenario simply needs to point at the correct individual id; `setScenario()` updates it in memory (call `saveProject()` when you want the fix on disk):

```{r}
setScenario(broken, "aciclovir_iv", individual = "adult_male")
```

Re-validate to confirm the project is clean again:

```{r}
fixed_results <- validateProject(broken)
fixed_results
isAnyCriticalErrors(fixed_results)
```

Both the report and `isAnyCriticalErrors()` are clean: every reference resolves and no required field is missing. Validation does not open the model file, so some problems still show up only when a scenario is built: a parameter path that does not exist in the model, a missing model file (reported only as a warning), a human individual or population without a `population`, a protein ontogeny that cannot be applied, or a human individual used with an animal model.

## Where to go next

With a clean project in hand, see `vignette("how-to-run-simulations")` to execute the scenarios and `vignette("how-to-plot-results")` to turn the results into figures. To write or repair the definitions a validation problem points at, see `vignette("how-to-design-scenarios")`.

To look up which fields a definition requires, see `vignette("reference-definition-fields")`. For why validation reports two levels and checks a different slice of the project per entry point, see `vignette("about-the-project-model")`.
